paragraphs: Non-convex optimization can use negative curvature to find directions that help move toward a second-order stationary point. Existing negative curvature descent methods estimate the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian, which describes local curvature. Requiring very accurate estimates throughout optimization can make this work expensive, especially when the desired final solution has a strict curvature tolerance.

The paper proposes adapting the accuracy of this estimate to the magnitude of the current gradient. It also makes a noisy negative curvature step compete with a gradient descent step. Together, these changes allow the algorithm to adjust how much effort it spends examining curvature as optimization progresses, instead of always using the same demanding precision target.

The authors consider both deterministic and stochastic optimization. Their analysis shows that adaptive negative curvature descent can reduce the total work needed to compute negative curvature without worsening iteration complexity. The distinction matters: the benefit concerns the cost of the work within optimization, while preserving the stated bound on the number of iterations.
neurips-2018-adaptive-negative-curvature.tldr: Adapting curvature-estimation accuracy to the current gradient can reduce non-convex optimization costs without sacrificing iteration complexity.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling is analyzed here through Bayesian regret, a measure of the accumulated cost of decisions relative to an optimal choice, averaged over prior uncertainty. Earlier information-theoretic bounds express this uncertainty using entropy. The difficulty is that entropy can grow arbitrarily large as the number of available actions increases, making the resulting guarantees less useful.

The paper replaces this dependence with a notion of rate-distortion. This changes how the analysis accounts for uncertainty: the relevant information requirement reflects a tradeoff involving decision quality, rather than relying directly on the entropy term. The contribution is a new set of theoretical bounds for understanding Thompson sampling when there are many actions.

For linear bandits, the authors recover a near-optimal bound using information-theoretic arguments. For logistic bandits, they obtain a bound that substantially improves on the previously available result. That second finding carries an explicit qualification: its information-theoretic statistic has only been quantified computationally. The improved logistic guarantee therefore retains a dependence whose size is assessed through computation.
neurips-2018-an-information-theoretic-an.tldr: Rate-distortion-based analysis yields stronger Thompson sampling regret bounds for settings with many actions.

paragraphs: Image matching and retrieval need representations that distinguish image patches while remaining compact. BinGAN addresses this by training a generative adversarial network to produce binary descriptors. Its starting point is the dimensionality reduction already present inside the discriminator: later layers offer a smaller representation of information expressed in earlier, higher-dimensional layers.

The method binarizes the discriminator's penultimate layer and trains this compact representation to mimic the distribution of the preceding representations. Two additional loss terms guide that process. One aims to reduce correlations among the binary dimensions, encouraging the descriptor to use its available capacity. The other transfers relationships between dimensions from the higher-dimensional representation into the smaller one.

These objectives connect compactness with the preservation of discriminative structure. Simply making a representation binary would not express both goals; the proposed regularization explicitly trains for them. The authors evaluate the descriptors on image matching and retrieval and report state-of-the-art results. The stated evidence therefore concerns the usefulness of the learned binary descriptors in those two applications.
neurips-2018-bingan-learning-compact-bin.tldr: BinGAN regularizes a GAN discriminator to learn compact binary image descriptors that preserve useful higher-dimensional relationships.

paragraphs: Distributed training repeatedly exchanges gradients between machines, so network performance can strongly affect how quickly training finishes. BML addresses this communication step with a gradient synchronization algorithm designed for a BCube network. The proposal joins an algorithmic choice with a network topology choice, making the communication infrastructure part of the training-speed solution.

The theoretical comparison is against a parameter server algorithm running on a Fat-Tree network with the same number of server machines. In that comparison, BML achieves one divided by k times the synchronization time while using k divided by five times as many switches. The abstract gives two to four as typical values of k.

The authors also test LeNet-5 and VGG-19 training on nine servers, each equipped with two GPUs. They report reductions in total training job completion time of up to 56.4%. This complements the synchronization analysis with an end-to-end measurement, while the phrase 'up to' identifies the largest reported improvement rather than a uniform reduction across every experiment.
neurips-2018-bml-a-high-performance-low-.tldr: BML combines gradient synchronization with BCube networking to reduce communication cost and accelerate distributed training.

paragraphs: CapProNet develops the capsule-network idea of representing class evidence with a vector. It learns a separate subspace associated with each class and projects an input feature vector onto these subspaces. The length of each resulting capsule supplies a score for the probability that the input belongs to the corresponding class.

Training learns an orthogonal projection matrix for every capsule subspace. The authors show that these subspaces are updated until they contain feature vectors associated with their classes. This gives the classifier a geometric interpretation: learning changes the spaces onto which features are projected, and the resulting vector lengths express class membership evidence.

The computational design uses low-dimensional capsule subspaces and an iterative approximation for a matrix inverse. The authors report that these choices add negligible training overhead. On image datasets, they report a 10–20% performance improvement for state-of-the-art ResNet backbones at almost the same computing cost. The abstract describes this as a performance improvement without identifying a more specific interpretation of that percentage.
neurips-2018-cappronet-deep-feature-lear.tldr: CapProNet scores classes using feature projections onto learned capsule subspaces, improving reported ResNet performance with little added computation.

paragraphs: Parallel statistical inference distributes computational work, but much of its existing theory assumes that data and parameters occupy ordinary Euclidean spaces. Some problems instead place them on manifolds, where the relevant geometry differs. The paper addresses this gap by extending parallel inference algorithms to optimization in these non-Euclidean settings.

The proposed algorithm combines communication efficiency with theoretical convergence guarantees. Both properties matter for distributed optimization: dividing computation across machines is useful only if exchanging information remains manageable and the combined procedure still progresses toward its optimization objective. The contribution brings these concerns together for problems whose geometry must be respected.

The authors demonstrate the method in two distinct settings. They estimate Fréchet means on simulated spherical data, providing an example of averaging in a curved space. They also apply low-rank matrix completion over Grassmann manifolds to the Netflix prize dataset. These applications show how the framework can address both explicitly geometric data and a matrix estimation problem represented through manifold optimization.
neurips-2018-communication-efficient-par.tldr: The paper extends parallel inference to manifold optimization with communication efficiency and theoretical convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Efficient reinforcement learning requires choosing which actions to explore, rather than relying entirely on random exploration. Optimistic methods use uncertainty to direct these choices, but many require substantial computation. This paper builds on least-squares temporal difference learning, whose summaries of past interactions offer a way to support informed exploration with incremental computation.

The authors derive upper confidence bounds for the action values learned by this method. A central feature is that the noise variance can depend on the state. Consequently, the exploration signal can distinguish between states with different levels of variability, concentrating exploration on some states while reducing it in others.

The resulting strategy is described as computationally efficient and incremental. It aims to capture some of the data-efficiency benefits associated with model-based methods while keeping computation closer to model-free approaches. Experiments show that it can converge faster than other incremental strategies that also use confidence estimates on action values. This is an empirical comparison supporting the value of accounting for state-dependent noise.
neurips-2018-context-dependent-upper-con.tldr: State-dependent confidence bounds guide reinforcement-learning exploration toward variable states while supporting efficient incremental updates.

paragraphs: Change-point detection asks where a stream of observations switches from one underlying distribution to another. The point of change is unknown and must be inferred from the data. This problem arises in settings such as biosurveillance, fault detection, finance, and security, where the observations can also contain personal information.

The paper studies this statistical task under differential privacy, a framework for providing worst-case privacy guarantees. Its contribution includes private algorithms for both online and offline detection. These cover two ways of handling the problem: looking for a change as observations arrive and analyzing a collection of observations after they have been gathered.

The authors analyze the algorithms theoretically and provide empirical validation of their results. The significance is the joint treatment of change detection and privacy: locating a distributional shift is studied with privacy protection built into the analysis. Covering both online and offline settings makes the contribution relevant to monitoring ongoing streams as well as examining historical data for a previously unknown change.
neurips-2018-differentially-private-chan.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates differentially private algorithms for detecting distributional changes in online and offline data.

paragraphs: DeepZ is a method and system for certifying neural network robustness. It uses abstract interpretation, which reasons about network behavior through approximations designed to support sound conclusions. The paper's central technical contribution is tailoring those approximations to neural networks so that certification can be both precise and computationally manageable.

The system supports feedforward and convolutional architectures, along with ReLU, Tanh, and Sigmoid activations. The authors report substantially better scalability and precision than state-of-the-art automated neural network verifiers. They also state that the method is sound with respect to floating-point arithmetic, connecting its guarantees to the numerical calculations actually used by the system.

One reported example involves a network with 88,500 hidden units. Under an L-infinity attack with epsilon equal to 0.1, DeepZ achieves 97% verification accuracy with an average runtime of 133 seconds. This example makes the scalability claim concrete for a specified network and perturbation setting. The reported verification accuracy concerns the certification result and should be read in that context.
neurips-2018-fast-and-effective-robustne.tldr: DeepZ uses neural-network-specific abstract interpretation to provide scalable robustness certification that accounts for floating-point arithmetic.

paragraphs: Deep neural networks depend heavily on large labeled datasets, and incorrect labels can hurt their performance. Mean absolute error has been proposed as a noise-robust replacement for categorical cross entropy, the commonly used training loss. This paper shows that mean absolute error can nevertheless perform poorly with deep networks and large datasets.

The authors introduce a theoretically grounded family of noise-robust losses that generalizes both mean absolute error and categorical cross entropy. This places the two existing choices within a broader formulation. The practical appeal is that the proposed losses can be applied with existing deep-network architectures and training algorithms, making the training objective the central point of intervention.

Experiments use CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and FASHION-MNIST with synthetically generated label noise. The authors report good performance across a broad range of these noisy-label scenarios. Their findings support the idea that designing the loss can help address label errors while avoiding the poor performance they identify for mean absolute error in the studied deep-learning settings.
neurips-2018-generalized-cross-entropy-l.tldr: A family of losses generalizing cross entropy and mean absolute error improves training across studied noisy-label scenarios.

paragraphs: Language encoding models predict brain responses from the language that elicited them. Models based on independent word embeddings leave out how surrounding language changes a word's interpretation. This paper instead uses contextual representations from an LSTM language model to build predictors of brain responses, allowing the representation of a stimulus to incorporate its context.

The authors report significantly improved encoding performance relative to state-of-the-art embeddings in nearly every brain area. They investigate the source of this improvement by changing how much context the models receive and by distorting that context. These comparisons attribute the gains to both improved word embeddings learned by the LSTM and the contextual information it supplies.

The models also allow the authors to map sensitivity to context across the cortex. Together, the results suggest a relationship between the high-level representations learned by LSTM language models and representations in the human brain. That conclusion is a suggested correspondence grounded in predictive performance and context manipulations, preserving the exploratory strength of the paper's interpretation.
neurips-2018-incorporating-context-into-.tldr: LSTM-derived contextual language representations improve brain-response prediction and help map cortical sensitivity to context.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing payments should encourage financially motivated workers to produce accurate labels. Static incentive mechanisms often assume prior knowledge of worker expertise or effort costs. This paper introduces a sequential mechanism that learns from collected labels without requiring that prior worker-model knowledge, allowing payment decisions to respond to evidence gathered over time.

A Bayesian inference algorithm augmented with Gibbs sampling first estimates workers' labeling strategies. Reinforcement incentive learning then uses these estimates to learn how workers respond to different payments. The mechanism adjusts payments dynamically without access to ground-truth labels, joining inference about worker behavior with learning how incentives influence that behavior.

The authors prove that the mechanism can encourage rational workers to supply high-quality labels both at individual steps and over the long run. Experiments also report consistently good performance for rational workers and workers modeled through adaptive learning. Compared with existing one-shot mechanisms, the offered payments are more robust and have lower variance. The theoretical rational-worker result and the broader empirical findings provide distinct forms of support.
neurips-2018-inference-aided-reinforceme.tldr: Bayesian worker inference and reinforcement learning jointly adapt crowdsourcing payments without requiring ground-truth labels or prior worker-model knowledge.

paragraphs: Structured prediction chooses outputs with multiple related parts. Standard margin-based training considers the maximum loss across possible outputs, and adding latent variables enlarges the search while introducing non-convexity. This paper extends an approach that replaces exhaustive output consideration with independently sampled structured outputs, bringing latent variables into that framework.

The authors study a family of loss functions under Gaussian perturbations and analyze how the latent space affects generalization bounds. They also connect non-convexity to a tight upper bound on Gibbs decoder distortion with respect to the latent space. This gives the difficult optimization structure a specific theoretical explanation within the proposed analysis.

A further formulation combines random samples and relaxations to produce a tighter upper bound on decoder distortion up to statistical accuracy. It permits polynomial-time evaluation of the objective function, addressing the cost of evaluating training criteria over large output and latent spaces. The authors illustrate the approach through synthetic experiments and a computer vision application; the computational claim specifically concerns objective evaluation.
neurips-2018-learning-latent-variable-st.tldr: Gaussian perturbations, sampling, and relaxations support latent-variable structured prediction with analyzed bounds and polynomial-time objective evaluation.

paragraphs: Efficient convolutional networks need to make good use of limited memory and computation. Many compact-network methods reduce filters through smaller, sparse, or binary representations. This paper introduces versatile filters, which take an additive approach: a primary filter contains the basis for a series of secondary filters that can be derived from it.

Those secondary filters do not require additional filter storage. When unfolded during computation, they can combine information extracted from different receptive fields, increasing the capability of the stored filter. The authors investigate this idea in both spatial and channel dimensions and describe the techniques as applicable to filters in existing convolutional networks.

Experiments across benchmark datasets and networks show comparable accuracy to the original filters with lower memory requirements and fewer floating-point operations. The result matters because it connects a richer use of stored filter information with overall resource savings. The secondary filters provide multiple computational uses of the underlying representation, while the reported network-level comparisons assess whether that design preserves accuracy efficiently.
neurips-2018-learning-versatile-filters-.tldr: Versatile filters derive multiple secondary filters from shared stored weights, preserving reported accuracy while reducing memory and computation.

paragraphs: LF-Net learns a local image-feature pipeline from scratch without human supervision. Its training signal comes from geometric information: depth and relative camera pose connect different images. Given the network's output on one image, these cues create a virtual target for what the network should produce on another image.

Constructing that target involves a non-differentiable process, which complicates gradient-based training. The authors handle this with two branches, confining the non-differentiable operation to one while preserving differentiability in the other. This arrangement makes it possible to optimize the network using targets derived from the relationship between images.

The method is trained on indoor and outdoor datasets. Indoor depth comes from 3D sensors, while outdoor depth is estimated using an existing Structure-from-Motion solution. Thus, the absence of human supervision is paired with access to geometric cues. The reported models outperform the state of the art in sparse feature matching on both datasets and run at more than 60 frames per second for QVGA images.
neurips-2018-lf-net-learning-local-featu.tldr: LF-Net uses depth, camera pose, and two-branch training to learn fast local image features without human supervision.

paragraphs: Large data tables can mix binary measurements, numbers, and counts while also containing missing entries. Low-rank models are useful for analyzing such tables, but the paper identifies a gap in methods combining statistical guarantees and efficient optimization: they do not explicitly represent additive row, column, or covariate effects alongside interactions.

LORIS combines low-rank interactions with sparse additive effects. It uses matrix regression on a dictionary together with a low-rank design to estimate both components simultaneously. This separates two kinds of structure within one model: main effects described by the additive component and interactions represented through the low-rank component.

The authors provide upper bounds on the estimation errors of both components. They also introduce mixed coordinate gradient descent, an algorithm with a proved sublinear convergence rate to an optimal solution and computational efficiency for large datasets. Results on simulated and survey data show an advantage over current practices. The contribution therefore includes a richer model, statistical error analysis, and an optimization method for fitting it.
neurips-2018-low-rank-interaction-with-s.tldr: LORIS jointly estimates sparse additive effects and low-rank interactions in heterogeneous tables, with statistical and optimization guarantees.

paragraphs: MAPO uses a memory of promising action sequences to reduce variance in policy-gradient estimates. It applies to deterministic environments with discrete actions, including structured prediction and combinatorial optimization. The motivation is particularly relevant when rewards are sparse: useful trajectories can be difficult to discover, making effective reuse of them valuable.

The method expresses expected return as a weighted combination of two expectations, one over high-reward trajectories in memory and another over trajectories outside it. Memory weight clipping helps accelerate and stabilize training, systematic exploration seeks additional high-reward trajectories, and distributed sampling from both groups supports larger-scale training.

The authors report improved sample efficiency and robustness, evaluating MAPO on weakly supervised program synthesis from natural language. It reaches 46.3% accuracy on WikiTableQuestions, with a reported 2.6% improvement over the state of the art. On WikiSQL it reaches 74.9% accuracy with weak supervision, exceeding several strong fully supervised baselines. These results demonstrate the memory-based approach in semantic parsing under the stated environment setting.
neurips-2018-memory-augmented-policy-opt.tldr: MAPO reuses high-reward trajectories through a memory buffer to improve policy-gradient learning, especially when rewards are sparse.

paragraphs: Choosing a neural network architecture requires expensive training and validation evaluations. Bayesian optimization is designed for objectives accessible through such costly evaluations, but conventional approaches focus on Euclidean or categorical search spaces. Those formulations naturally accommodate scalar hyperparameters and make searching over network architectures a separate challenge.

NASBOT extends Gaussian-process-based Bayesian optimization to architecture search. Its central ingredient is a distance between neural network architectures that can be computed efficiently using an optimal transport program. Providing this notion of architectural similarity gives the optimization framework a way to work with networks as structured candidates in its search space.

The authors evaluate NASBOT on several model-selection tasks using cross-validation, covering multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks. They report that it outperforms the alternative architecture-search methods considered. The distance itself is also proposed as potentially useful beyond Bayesian optimization. That broader role is presented as a possible application, while the empirical findings concern the architecture-search tasks evaluated in the paper.
neurips-2018-neural-architecture-search-.tldr: NASBOT uses an optimal-transport distance between architectures to enable Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization of neural networks.

paragraphs: Non-local image methods use similarities between different parts of a signal to help process it. Many select the nearest neighbors in a fixed feature space, but the discrete selection rule makes it difficult to learn that space directly for the application. The paper addresses this obstacle by replacing hard neighbor selection with a differentiable relaxation.

The relaxation is continuous and deterministic, and remains differentiable with respect to pairwise distances. A temperature parameter controls its behavior, with ordinary nearest-neighbor selection recovered as the temperature approaches zero. The authors incorporate this mechanism into the neural nearest neighbors block, or N3 block, which can serve as a non-local layer inside a neural network.

The block lets networks exploit self-similarity while making the matching representation amenable to optimization. The authors demonstrate effectiveness on correspondence classification, image denoising, and single-image super-resolution. For image restoration, they report outperforming strong convolutional baselines and recent non-local models using nearest-neighbor selection in hand-chosen feature spaces. These findings support learning the matching process together with the application.
neurips-2018-neural-nearest-neighbors-ne.tldr: A differentiable relaxation of nearest-neighbor selection lets neural networks learn non-local matching for restoration and correspondence tasks.

paragraphs: Neural networks can lose previously learned capabilities when trained on successive tasks, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. This paper approaches the problem through Bayesian online learning. After each task, it approximates the posterior distribution over network weights with a Gaussian and carries that approximation forward into learning the next task.

The resulting procedure introduces a quadratic penalty on weight changes. Constructing the Laplace approximation requires curvature information around a mode, normally involving a Hessian that is impractical to compute for modern networks. The authors make the method scalable through block-diagonal, Kronecker-factored approximations to this curvature.

This design connects information retained from earlier tasks with a structured, computationally manageable constraint on later weight updates. In experiments, the algorithm achieves more than 90% test accuracy across a sequence of 50 versions of permuted MNIST and substantially outperforms related methods for catastrophic forgetting. The result supports the approach on that sequential benchmark, while the methodological contribution is the scalable online approximation used to retain previous learning.
neurips-2018-online-structured-laplace-a.tldr: A scalable structured Gaussian approximation carries information between tasks to reduce catastrophic forgetting in neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose decisions when the objective is uncertain and the available evidence consists of observational data. Decisions can vary continuously and involve several dimensions at once. The task therefore goes beyond choosing among a small set of fixed alternatives: a method must search a richer decision space using information extracted from existing observations.

The proposed framework uses predictive machine learning and incorporates uncertainty about predicted outcomes into the decision process. Its purpose is prescriptive: predictions support choosing what to do. Accounting for uncertainty makes the reliability of a predicted outcome part of the information used when selecting a decision.

The authors describe the framework as computationally tractable and asymptotically consistent, providing a theoretical basis for its behavior as data increase. They also demonstrate it on examples involving synthetic and real datasets, reporting better performance than comparable methods on those problems. The contribution combines predictive modeling, uncertainty information, and optimization within one approach to decision-making from observational evidence.
neurips-2018-optimization-over-continuou.tldr: The framework combines predictive models and outcome uncertainty to optimize continuous, multidimensional decisions from observational data.

paragraphs: Event data record occurrences at irregular times, making relationships between event types central to understanding the sequence. Proximal graphical event models represent those relationships through parent sets. The occurrence rate of an event type depends only on whether its parent event types have appeared within the relevant recent history.

The method learns both which event types act as parents and the time windows used to define that history. This makes the representation entirely data driven, avoiding additional user choices such as basis functions or hyperparameters that can require domain expertise in other graphical event models. The learned windows specify how recent an event must be to count.

The authors theoretically justify learning optimal history windows and parent sets, and state soundness and completeness results for parent-structure learning. They also introduce efficient heuristics and demonstrate their effectiveness on synthetic and real datasets. The contribution combines a specific recent-history model with a learning procedure that reduces the need for manually supplied modeling choices.
neurips-2018-proximal-graphical-event-mo.tldr: PGEMs learn event dependencies and relevant history windows directly from irregular event data.

paragraphs: Sparse learning is useful for large, high-dimensional datasets, and L1 regularization is a common way to encourage sparsity. This paper introduces proximal SCOPE, or pSCOPE, for carrying out that learning across multiple machines. The method uses a cooperative autonomous local learning framework, allowing local learning to contribute to a distributed procedure.

A central finding is that the way data are partitioned across machines affects convergence. The authors define a metric for partition quality and use it to prove a linear convergence rate when the partition is sufficiently good. They also prove that better partitions lead to faster convergence, connecting data placement directly to the behavior of the optimization algorithm.

The guarantee is conditional on partition quality, making that quality an explicit part of the method's analysis. The authors additionally describe pSCOPE as communication efficient. Experiments on real datasets show that it can outperform other state-of-the-art distributed sparse-learning methods. Together, the theoretical and empirical results highlight both algorithm design and data partitioning as contributors to efficient distributed learning.
neurips-2018-proximal-scope-for-distribu.tldr: pSCOPE enables communication-efficient distributed sparse learning with linear convergence when data partitions are sufficiently good.

paragraphs: Combining model-based and model-free reinforcement learning promises strong performance with fewer interactions with the environment. The difficulty is that a learned dynamics model is imperfect, especially in complex environments. Predictions generated by that model can introduce errors into learning, potentially undermining the benefit of using simulated experience.

Stochastic ensemble value expansion, or STEVE, addresses this by dynamically interpolating between model rollouts of different lengths. A rollout uses the model to predict a sequence of future steps. Combining different horizons allows the procedure to adjust how extensively it relies on model predictions, using the model only when doing so does not introduce significant errors.

The authors evaluate STEVE on challenging continuous-control benchmarks and report outperforming model-free baselines with an order-of-magnitude improvement in sample efficiency. The findings support adaptive use of model predictions as a way to gain more learning from limited environment interaction. The central contribution is controlling the extent of model use so that prediction errors do not erase its efficiency benefits.
neurips-2018-sample-efficient-reinforcem.tldr: STEVE adaptively combines model rollouts of different lengths to improve sample efficiency while controlling model-induced errors.

paragraphs: The authors study repeated human choices among options with uncertain rewards in a stationary bandit experiment. They vary the average abundance and variability of rewards. At the end of a game, participants' reported expectations for unchosen options reveal a significant underestimate of the prior mean reward rate, which the paper calls pessimism bias.

A Dynamic Belief Model fitted to choices captures this bias well, despite assuming that reward rates can change when they are actually fixed. A Fixed Belief Model with the correct stationary assumption captures it poorly, and a simple reinforcement-learning model captures it incompletely. The comparison links the observed pessimism to how participants may represent the environment.

Simulations show that an underestimated prior mean can improve long-term gain when an observer assumes volatility in a stable environment and uses a softmax decision policy. This conditional result suggests that pessimism might compensate for an incorrect environmental assumption and a simplified choice rule. It offers a possible explanation of the behavior rather than establishing that pessimism is generally optimal.
neurips-2018-why-so-gloomy-a-bayesian-ex.tldr: Human reward pessimism may compensate for assumed environmental volatility and a simplified decision policy in stationary bandit tasks.
